questions.topic: Origin of the B. diminuta challenge
questions.question: What did Frances Bowman of the FDA observe in 1960 that led to the development of ASTM F838?

options.A: A 0.2 µm membrane was penetrated by Serratia marcescens at a 10^7 CFU/cm² challenge, leading to a radiation sterilization standard
options.B: Media filtered through 0.45 µm was still contaminated, with the organism able to penetrate in small numbers above 10^4-10^6 CFU/cm²
options.C: A 0.45 µm membrane released fibers into the filtrate during filtration, leading to the USP nonfiber release test
options.D: A 0.22 µm membrane could not retain virus particles, leading to a separate guideline on filtration as a virus clearance step

questions.explanation: Early 0.45 µm membranes were regarded as sterilizing-grade and confirmed using Serratia marcescens; Bowman found that media filtered through 0.45 µm was contaminated by a very small bacterium that could penetrate in small numbers above 10^4-10^6 CFU/cm², which directly led to the development of ASTM F838. Serratia was the early confirmation organism, not the organism observed to penetrate; fiber release and viruses are not the focus of this history.

questions.question: According to TR26, which of the following is not an intended target of sterilizing filtration?

options.A: Bacteria, such as Brevundimonas diminuta
options.B: Fungi such as yeast and mold
options.C: Process bioburden microorganisms
options.D: Viruses

questions.explanation: The TR26 introduction notes specifically that sterilizing filtration is not intended to remove viruses. The aim of sterilizing filtration is to remove microorganisms from a liquid without affecting product quality.

questions.question: To which type of filtration process do the concepts of TR26 mainly apply?

options.A: Processes that use filtration to render a liquid sterile with the corresponding assurance; not necessarily applicable to upstream bioburden reduction steps
options.B: All pharmaceutical filtration steps, including upstream bioburden reduction, chromatography column protection, and buffer and media filtration
options.C: Only sterilizing filtration of gases such as compressed air and nitrogen and of tank vents
options.D: Only the final sterilizing filtration of marketed products in regions under US FDA jurisdiction

questions.explanation: Section 1.1 states that the concepts of TR26 address processes that use filtration to render a liquid sterile with all the corresponding assurance, and may not apply universally to all filtration, for example upstream bioburden reduction steps. The topic of TR26 is liquid filtration rather than gases; the revision team and reviewers came from Europe, the US, and Asia-Pacific, and the content is designed to be globally applicable rather than limited to FDA jurisdiction.

questions.question: Which statement about how TR26 positions itself is correct?

options.A: It is a mandatory standard, and failure to follow it constitutes a GMP deficiency requiring a deviation investigation
options.B: It is written entirely according to EU GMP Annex 1 and applies only to aseptic manufacturers within the EU
options.C: It is a scientific guide that does not establish mandatory standards and does not necessarily cover region-specific regulatory expectations
options.D: It replaces ASTM F838 and becomes the sole basis for grading sterilizing-grade membranes

questions.explanation: Section 1.1 explains that this report should be regarded as a guide, is not intended to establish mandatory standards for sterilizing filtration, and does not necessarily address region-specific regulatory expectations, but provides current scientific recommendations that industry and regulators can use in developing sterilizing filtration policies. ASTM F838 remains the standard method on which sterilizing-grade classification is based.

questions.question: What is one of the main purposes of this edition (Revised 2025) of TR26?

options.A: To reflect current best practices and regulatory expectations, and to clarify the respective roles of filter suppliers and end-users
options.B: To redefine 0.45 µm membranes as sterilizing-grade in order to increase flow rate for high-viscosity products
options.C: To add a validation method for virus removal with sterilizing filters and specify minimum log reduction requirements
options.D: To abolish the bacterial retention study and prove sterility directly from integrity test results

questions.explanation: The original TR26 was issued in 1998 and revised in 2008; this edition was prepared to reflect current best practices and regulatory expectations and to clarify the roles of the filter supplier and the end-user. 0.45 µm has long since stopped being regarded as sterilizing-grade because of Bowman's finding; virus removal is out of scope; and the bacterial retention study remains the core of validation, with the integrity test only a correlated surrogate check.

questions.question: According to the TR26 Glossary, what is meant by "Double Filtration" (also called Additive Filtration)?

options.A: A second filter serves as a backup and needs to be tested only when the primary filter fails its integrity test
options.B: Two filters of decreasing pore size are placed in series, and only the most downstream one needs bacterial retention validation
options.C: Both filters in series must be present to achieve sterility, so both must pass the post-use integrity test
options.D: The same filter filters the same batch of product twice in succession to raise the sterility assurance level

questions.explanation: Double filtration is two filters in series where, according to process-specific bacterial retention validation, both are necessary to obtain a sterile filtrate, so both must meet the post-use integrity test specification. "The second serves as a backup" describes redundant filtration; "decreasing pore sizes in series" is closer to ordinary serial filtration; and repeat filtration through the same filter is not what the term means.
questions.reference: PDA TR26 §2.0 Glossary (Double / Redundant / Serial Filtration)

questions.question: How does the TR26 Glossary define "Integrity Test"?

options.A: A nondestructive physical test that can be correlated with the bacterial retention capability of the filter/filter assembly
options.B: A destructive microbiological test that challenges the filter with B. diminuta and needs days of incubation to read
options.C: A filterability test that measures the maximum product volume a filter can process before plugging
options.D: A chemical test that analyzes the extractables content of filter flush fluid by TOC or LC-MS

questions.explanation: An integrity test is a nondestructive physical test whose value is that it can be correlated with bacterial retention capability, so it can be run on every production filter. The test that challenges with B. diminuta is the bacterial retention study (destructive, not usable on routine production filters); the test measuring volume before plugging is a filterability test; and analyzing flush fluid for extractables belongs to extractables assessment.

questions.question: Which statement about the difference between an extractable and a leachable is correct?

options.A: An extractable is a component that migrates into the product during storage or normal use; a leachable is a component extracted under exaggerated conditions such as solvent and temperature
options.B: The two are synonyms, differing only in the habitual usage of filter suppliers and pharmaceutical users, and are interchangeable
options.C: A leachable comes only from O-rings and housings, and an extractable only from the polymer of the membrane itself
options.D: An extractable is a component that moves out under exaggerated conditions such as solvent, temperature, and time; a leachable is a component that migrates into the product during normal use

questions.explanation: An extractable is a chemical component moved out of a material by artificial or exaggerated means (solvent, temperature, time); a leachable is a component that migrates from the contact surface into the drug product or process fluid under storage or normal use conditions, and is usually a subset of the extractables. The option with the two definitions swapped is wrong; they are not synonyms; and both the membrane and device components can be sources of either.

questions.question: According to the Glossary, what generally needs to be done for a hydrophobic membrane to pass water at a low pressure differential?

options.A: Soak it in hot WFI for at least 30 minutes first, converting the membrane to hydrophilic
options.B: Pre-wet the membrane first with a low surface tension liquid (for example alcohol)
options.C: Use a higher test pressure for the bubble point test to open the pores
options.D: Nothing is needed, as a hydrophobic membrane naturally lets water flow at low pressure differential

questions.explanation: A hydrophobic membrane repels high surface tension liquids such as water and cannot be wetted unless a high pressure differential is applied; if it is pre-wetted with a low surface tension liquid such as alcohol, water can pass at low pressure differential. Hot WFI soaking does not change its hydrophobicity; raising the bubble point test pressure is not a wetting method; and "nothing needed" is the opposite of the definition.

questions.question: According to the Glossary, what is the typical manifestation of membrane fouling?

options.A: Flux rises at constant pressure, because the pores are flushed open and resistance falls
options.B: Flux falls at constant pressure, or differential pressure rises at constant flux
options.C: Differential pressure falls continually at constant flux, indicating that membrane resistance and system load are gradually easing
options.D: Bubble point gradually decreases with filtration time, indicating that the pore size is growing

questions.explanation: Fouling is the result of solutes plugging or masking membrane pores, and appears as a fall in flux at constant pressure or a rise in filtration differential pressure at constant flux (section 5.2.1 also notes that a rising pressure differential at constant flow indicates fouling). "Flux rises at constant pressure" and "pressure falls at constant flux" are the opposite direction; fouling that blocks large pores tends to raise the bubble point instead (section 7.5.1), not lower it.

questions.question: How does TR26 describe the mechanisms by which a sterilizing-grade membrane retains microorganisms?

options.A: Purely sieve-type size exclusion, with all particles stopped at the upstream surface
options.B: Mainly the charge on the membrane surface killing microorganisms rather than retaining them
options.C: The membrane is made of cylindrical pores of uniform diameter, so anything larger than the pore size is fully retained
options.D: In addition to surface sieving and deep-layer retention by size exclusion, there is an adsorptive retention mechanism

questions.explanation: Section 3.0 states that the membrane is a sponge-like, deep-layer structure with a distribution of pore sizes: large particles are sieved at the surface, marginally sized particles are retained within the depth, and there is also adsorptive sequestration, in which small particles that could pass through the pores are still adsorbed by chemical or physical interactions. Treating the membrane as a simple screen or as uniform cylindrical pores is an oversimplification that TR26 explicitly points out; adsorption retains rather than kills.

questions.question: Why does TR26 say that complete retention of small microorganisms can be "probabilistic", so that it must be validated for each application?

options.A: Because membrane pores grow by a fixed 10% or so after each use and need to be reassessed
options.B: Because microorganisms grow, shrink, deform, and divide, and adsorptive retention is affected by conditions such as pressure differential, flow rate, pH, and ionic strength
options.C: Because the integrity test itself has a high false-positive rate and cannot alone determine whether the filter fully retains
options.D: Because modern sterilizing filters lack manufacturing control and have no safety margin

questions.explanation: For particles much larger than all pores, retention is independent of process conditions; but small microorganisms grow, shrink, deform, and divide, and the effect of adsorptive retention depends on pressure differential, flow rate, particle number, saturation of binding sites, and liquid surface tension, pH, and ionic strength, making complete retention a probabilistic property of the process and filter, so it must be validated for the application. TR26 in fact points out that modern sterilizing filters have well-established manufacturing controls and a significant safety margin; the other options are not TR26's reasons.

questions.question: On what basis does the industry consensus define a "sterilizing-grade filter"?

options.A: Actual measurement of membrane cross-sections by SEM or porometry, confirming that the maximum pore size does not exceed 0.2 µm and is uniformly distributed
options.B: A bubble point value above a fixed pressure threshold set by the manufacturer
options.C: Reproducible retention of 10^7 CFU/cm² of B. diminuta according to ASTM F838
options.D: A USP particle test showing no particles >10 µm in the filtrate

questions.explanation: Section 3.1 states that the industry consensus does not define sterilizing-grade by physical pore size measurement, but by whether the filter reproducibly retains 10^7 CFU of Brevundimonas diminuta per cm² according to ASTM F838. A rating such as 0.2 µm can even be given without any pore size measurement; bubble point and particle tests are other quality attributes.

questions.question: In Table 3.1-1, what is the difference between a "sterilizing filter" and a "sterilizing-grade filter"?

options.A: A sterilizing filter is one for which process-specific validation has been completed in a specific application and for which sterility of the filtrate is claimed
options.B: The two are fully synonymous, and supplier catalogs and user documents can use them interchangeably
options.C: A sterilizing filter is one that has itself been steam or radiation sterilized and is in a sterile state
options.D: The term sterilizing-grade filter may be used only for filters for which the user has completed process-specific validation and has claimed sterility of the filtrate

questions.explanation: A sterilizing-grade filter is the supplier's claim about the filter itself according to ASTM F838, independent of any specific application; a sterilizing filter additionally claims that the filter truly renders the liquid sterile in a specific application, requiring completion of process-specific validation and other controls, and using the term means making a sterility claim for the filtrate. "The filter itself has been sterilized and is in a sterile state" is the confusion that the term "sterile filter" can cause, and TR26 recommends avoiding it.

questions.question: Which statement about the "0.2 µm or 0.22 µm rated filter" designation is correct?

options.A: 0.2 µm and 0.22 µm are two different grades, and the retention capability of 0.22 µm is clearly poorer
options.B: As long as it is labeled 0.2 µm, the filter is guaranteed to have passed the ASTM F838 retention test
options.C: It may be given according to other standards, and even for filters used only for bioburden reduction
options.D: It means the supplier has actually measured and released the true pore size of every filter

questions.explanation: Table 3.1-1 explains that a 0.2/0.22 µm designation may be given on the basis of passing ASTM F838, but may also be given according to other criteria, even for filters used only for bioburden reduction or that have not passed F838, so "sterilizing-grade filter" is the more precise term. 0.2 and 0.22 µm are treated as interchangeable nominal pore sizes; and a pore size rating can be given without any physical pore size measurement.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the qualification documents provided by a filter manufacturer (validation guide, DMF, and so on) and user validation?

options.A: They can support, but cannot replace, the performance qualification the user performs in process validation
options.B: They can completely replace the user's validation, with the user needing only to file them and show them at audits
options.C: They can be cited only when the product is a small molecule, no single-use system is used, and the filter and housing are from the same supplier
options.D: They are only for reference in purchasing selection and no manufacturer data can be cited in regulatory filings

questions.explanation: Section 4.1 states clearly that the manufacturer's qualification documents "support but do not replace" the filter user's performance qualification in process validation; the documents can also help the user evaluate the filter and respond to regulatory questions. So they can neither completely replace it nor are they uncitable; the document sets no small molecule or SUS restriction.

questions.topic: Tests not repeated by the user
questions.question: According to 4.1, which of the following is generally completed by the filter manufacturer and does not need to be repeated by the user?

options.A: Bacterial retention testing with the actual product
options.B: Establishing product-wetted integrity test limits
options.C: Filter safety testing such as biological reactivity
options.D: Assessing whether a leachables study is needed based on extractables results

questions.explanation: Section 4.1 states that filter safety testing (biological reactivity) is performed by the manufacturer and need not be repeated by the user. In Table 4.1-1, bacterial retention in product and product integrity test are marked V (user process validation), and leachables is marked E (the user evaluates the need and documents a technical assessment).

questions.question: In the 4.5 filter cleanliness assessment, which particle sizes are checked in the filter flush effluent?

options.A: Particles larger than 0.2 µm and larger than 0.45 µm
options.B: Particles larger than 10 µm and larger than 25 µm
options.C: Particles larger than 50 µm and larger than 100 µm
options.D: Only visible foreign matter is checked, without counting

questions.explanation: The filter flush effluent is checked for particles >10 µm and >25 µm, and meeting the pharmacopoeial particulate matter requirements for injections is considered acceptable, which is how nonfiber-releasing is confirmed. 0.2/0.45 µm are membrane pore size ratings, not particle inspection thresholds.

questions.question: What does TR26 recommend regarding filter chemical compatibility?

options.A: The manufacturer's compatibility table is sufficient, and the user need not do any testing
options.B: Passing a single integrity test is enough to judge full compatibility with the product
options.C: Only the membrane itself needs to be assessed, without including components such as the housing and O-rings
options.D: The manufacturer's table is only a starting point; the whole device should be assessed with a combination of tests

questions.explanation: Section 4.6.1 explains that the manufacturer's compatibility table often serves as the starting point for further testing, and the user should assess under process conditions; testing should cover the whole device and depend on the fluid, filtration temperature, and contact time. A combination of tests (integrity, tensile strength, NVR, extractables, SEM, burst pressure, and so on) is recommended, because a single test may fail to detect subtle incompatibility.

questions.question: Why do filters sterilized by gamma or x-ray irradiation have an expiration date?

options.A: Because irradiation causes the membrane pore size to gradually increase with storage time
options.B: Because the TSE risk from tallow derivatives rises with storage time
options.C: Because the manufacturer does not validate the packaging and shipping conditions for such filters
options.D: Because a sterility claim is associated with that sterilization method

questions.explanation: Section 4.8 states that filters sterilized by gamma or x-ray carry an expiration date because they come with a sterility claim associated with the sterilization method. TR26 does not say that pore size increases with time; section 4.4.2 explains that tallow-derived stearates essentially carry no TSE transmission risk; and manufacturers validate packaging and shipping according to industry standards.

questions.question: At what location should the pre-filtration bioburden sample be taken?

options.A: In the compounding tank, before any prefilter and bioburden reduction filter, to reflect the rawest and highest bioburden load
options.B: Immediately upstream of the sterilizing filter (upstream of the first filter if redundant), and downstream of any bioburden reduction filter
options.C: Downstream of the sterilizing filter and before the filling needle, to confirm that the filtrate has become sterile
options.D: Between the two redundant sterilizing filters, to monitor the load on both filters at once

questions.explanation: Section 5.6 states that the pre-filtration bioburden sample should be taken immediately upstream of the sterilizing filter; with redundant filtration, upstream of the first sterilizing filter and downstream of any bioburden reduction filter. This measures the load that actually enters the sterilizing filter. The sampling time should also be representative: sample at the end of filtration if the bioburden may rise.

questions.question: In a redundant filtration configuration, which filter should generally serve as the primary filter?

options.A: The filter closest to filling (the most downstream one)
options.B: The most upstream filter, the first to contact the product
options.C: The filter with the larger effective filtration area
options.D: The one decided by whichever has the better integrity test result for that batch

questions.explanation: Section 5.5.1.3 states that the filter closest to filling (the most downstream) should generally be the primary filter; the secondary filter is usually identical to the primary and is itself fully validated, serving as a backup if the primary fails. The role of the primary is defined at design, not chosen afterwards based on test results.

questions.question: What effect does an increase in process temperature have on a filter's maximum allowable differential pressure?

options.A: The higher the temperature, the higher the pressure rating, because the membrane becomes tougher when heated
options.B: No effect, since a filter's pressure rating depends only on pore size rating and housing material
options.C: It affects only the reverse flow direction, with the forward flow pressure rating unaffected by temperature
options.D: The higher the temperature, the lower the pressure rating; and reverse flow is generally regarded as the worst case

questions.explanation: Section 5.2.2 explains that rising temperature lowers the maximum allowable pressure differential because the mechanical strength of the filter structure falls, and Figure 5.2.2-1 shows that the higher the temperature, the lower the pressure rating. Pressure limits for forward and reverse directions may differ, with reverse flow often regarded as the worst case; both directions are affected by temperature. High temperature may also increase leachables and chemical incompatibility.

questions.question: What may be seen early in filtration of a protein formulation containing polysorbate, and what countermeasure does TR26 mention?

options.A: Protein concentration is initially high; the filtration flow rate should be reduced and the filtration time extended
options.B: Polysorbate concentration is abnormally high initially; the filter area should be increased and the filtrate diluted back to specification by flushing with a large volume of WFI
options.C: Polysorbate concentration is initially low; a flush buffer containing surfactant can be used to reduce the volume of product flush
options.D: Nothing changes; polysorbate does not adsorb to sterilizing membranes

questions.explanation: Section 5.7 states that adsorptive saturation of polysorbate and poloxamer on filter materials can be much slower than for proteins, leading to a low excipient concentration in the filtrate early in filtration; using a flush buffer containing surfactant can greatly reduce the product flush volume needed and raise yield. The flush volume can first be estimated at scale-down but must be confirmed at full scale, and a flush curve can be built with fractional collection plus TOC, excipient concentration, and so on.

questions.question: When using small-scale experiments to predict filtration performance at commercial scale, which of the following scale-up risks does TR26 specifically warn is easily overlooked?

options.A: If the test material has not gone through the same shear or freeze-thaw history as commercial scale, plugging at commercial scale may be underestimated
options.B: Small-scale results always overestimate commercial throughput by about ten times, so it must be divided by ten
options.C: As long as a 47 mm disc is used, scaling is linear, with no need to consider pleat density
options.D: A surrogate fluid is always more representative of fouling behavior than the actual product and should be used first

questions.explanation: Section 5.4.2 gives examples: protein subjected to shear stress upstream can form subvisible particles that cause plugging, while the same solution without that shear may show no fouling at all; freeze-thaw or shipping conditions for LNP and lentivirus also affect throughput, so test material must be representative of commercial. TR26 also points out that small-scale devices may not scale linearly because flow paths and pleat density differ, and that a surrogate may not represent fouling.

questions.question: What is the minimum bacterial challenge level for a process-specific bacterial retention study?

options.A: ≥ 1 × 10^7 CFU/mL of product
options.B: ≥ 1 × 10^4 CFU/cm² of effective filtration area
options.C: ≥ 1 × 10^7 CFU/cm² of filtration area
options.D: ≥ 1 × 10^6 CFU per test filter

questions.explanation: The challenge requirement is at least 1 × 10^7 CFU of B. diminuta (or an appropriate process isolate) per cm² of membrane area. This number derives from Bowman's observation that B. diminuta could penetrate a 0.45 µm membrane at >10^4-10^6 CFU/cm². TR26 specifically warns against confusing challenge concentration (CFU/mL) with challenge level (CFU/cm²).

questions.question: What is the purpose of placing a 0.45 µm filter in parallel in a bacterial retention study?

options.A: To serve as a prefilter, first lowering the challenge organism load so that the test filter does not plug
options.B: To collect its filtrate for extractables analysis, saving test product
options.C: To show that a 0.45 µm membrane can also serve as a backup sterilizing filter for the product
options.D: To serve as a positive control, confirming the size, dispersion, and viability of the organism

questions.explanation: Whatever test design is used, a 0.4/0.45 µm positive control filter should be run in parallel. Recovery of the challenge organism downstream of the 0.45 µm filter shows that it is small enough, monodispersed, and still viable, which is what gives the result of "no penetration" for the test filter its meaning. A 0.45 µm filter is not a sterilizing filter, nor a prefilter or a source of extractables samples.

questions.question: What does TR26 recommend about the selection of test membranes for a process-specific bacterial retention study?

options.A: Generally three membrane lots, with at least one lot having a pre-use integrity value as close as possible to the lower manufacturer specification limit
options.B: Three membranes from one membrane lot are enough, choosing those with the highest integrity values and tightest pores
options.C: Only full-size 10-inch production cartridges may be used, with membrane discs not permitted
options.D: Membranes must have been sterilized the same number of times under the user's actual SIP conditions

questions.explanation: Section 6.6.5 recommends including multiple membrane lots (generally three), with at least one lot having a pre-use integrity value as close as possible to the manufacturer's specification (the lowest specification membrane being defined by the manufacturer), so as to challenge the least favorable membrane. If only validating a membrane material, small discs are generally sufficient; section 6.6.1 also notes that the user's sterilization method generally need not be fully simulated.

questions.question: In the viability test, if the difference in viable counts between the product and the control over at least 30 minutes is less than about how much, can direct inoculation of the challenge organism into the product for the bacterial retention study be considered?

options.A: About 0.1 log
options.B: About 1 log
options.C: About 3 log
options.D: About 6 log

questions.explanation: Section 6.6.4 states that if the difference between test and control over at least 30 minutes is less than about 1 log, direct inoculation into the process fluid may be a feasible option; if viability has already fallen close to 1 log at the required time point, the exposure time may need to be shortened, otherwise the minimum challenge of ≥ 1 × 10^7 CFU/cm² may not be reached.

questions.question: How should the filtrate of a bacterial retention study be analyzed?

options.A: 100 mL taken at each of the beginning, middle, and end of filtration is enough to represent all the filtrate
options.B: All of the challenge filtrate must be analyzed, for example by passing it directly through a downstream analytical membrane
options.C: Only the last portion of filtrate needs testing, because bacterial penetration mostly occurs late in filtration
options.D: A passing post-use integrity test result directly replaces the microbiological culture analysis and reading of the filtrate

questions.explanation: Section 6.6.8 requires analysis of all the challenge filtrate, which can be passed directly through an analytical membrane downstream of the test filter (generally a maximum of 0.4 or 0.45 µm), or collected in a sterile container and then filtered. Taking only a portion is not enough, because the few cells that penetrate may be in the part not sampled and go undetected; an integrity test cannot replace this analysis.

questions.question: According to Table 7.1.1-1, which integrity test method is recommended when the effective filtration area is greater than about 1.8 m²?

options.A: Bubble point only, because it most directly reflects the maximum pore size
options.B: Pressure hold only, because the upstream volume of large systems is larger
options.C: Visual inspection of the cartridge appearance and O-rings in place of physical testing
options.D: Diffusive flow plus bubble point

questions.explanation: Reference values in Table 7.1.1-1: < 0.03 m² uses bubble point (diffusive flow is too small for the instrument to measure accurately); 0.03-1.8 m² can use bubble point or diffusive flow; > 1.8 m² uses a combination of diffusive flow and bubble point. At very large areas, the background diffusive flow can swamp the bubble point signal, so bubble point alone is not enough. These are approximate values, and the manufacturer's recommendation governs.

questions.question: Under what circumstances must a sterilizing filter undergo a post-use integrity test?

options.A: Only when PUPSIT has been registered with the regulatory authority for that process
options.B: Only when obvious fouling or a rise in pressure differential is observed during filtration
options.C: It is mandatory when the claimed purpose is sterilization
options.D: Only the manufacturer must test before shipment, and the user may omit it

questions.explanation: Section 7.5 states that where the claimed purpose is sterilization, a post-use integrity test is mandatory, to confirm that the filter remained integral throughout the period of use; if non-integrity is indeed detected, the root cause must be thoroughly investigated, and the batch is generally rejected (or reprocessed if validated). The manufacturer also tests each filter before shipment, but this cannot replace the user's post-use test.

questions.question: Which statement about TR26's position on PUPSIT is correct?

options.A: PUPSIT is mandatory in all regions and cannot be omitted from any process
options.B: A highly fouling fluid may mask defects; where PUPSIT is not feasible, the risk of not performing it must be managed by risk assessment
options.C: PUPSIT can replace the post-use integrity test, with either one being performed and no need for both
options.D: Serious large-area damage can also be masked by fouling, so PUPSIT must be done

questions.explanation: Section 7.5.1 explains that in extreme cases a highly fouling fluid can shift post-use results and mask defects, in which case PUPSIT can find flaws that post-use testing cannot detect; but this situation is uncommon in final filtration. PUPSIT is a common regulatory expectation, and where it is not feasible in the process, the risk of not performing PUPSIT must be assessed and managed through a complete risk assessment rather than used to rationalize omission. TR26 points out that severe damage cannot be masked, and post-use testing remains mandatory.

questions.question: After an integrity test failure, in the troubleshooting sequence of 7.6, what is the final step before the filter is judged unacceptable?

options.A: Retest with a lower surface tension reference fluid; if it still fails, judge it unacceptable
options.B: Judge it unacceptable on the first failure, discarding the filter directly and rejecting the batch
options.C: Keep raising the test pressure and rewetting and retesting until the instrument gives a passing result, with no limit on the number of attempts
options.D: Repeat the test with a different test gas such as CO2 until the result passes

questions.explanation: Section 7.6 first confirms test method, parameters, wetting fluid, absence of leaks, temperature stability, calibration, and the correct filter, then proceeds in order: rewet and retest, then stronger wetting conditions (more flush volume/time, differential pressure, or back pressure), then testing with a lower surface tension reference fluid; failure in the reference fluid is judged a failure. The number of permitted retests must be defined in advance and proceduralized, with no unlimited retesting or arbitrary changes to parameters.

questions.question: According to the bubble point ratio approach (Equation 1), how is the minimum product-wet bubble point (PBPmin) calculated?

options.A: PBPmin = WBPavg × (WBPmin ÷ PBPavg)
options.B: PBPmin = PBPavg − WBPmin
options.C: PBPmin = WBPmin × (PBPavg ÷ WBPavg)
options.D: PBPmin = WBPmin × (WBPavg ÷ PBPavg)

questions.explanation: Discs from at least three membrane lots are first tested for bubble point with water and then with product, and the ratio of the two averages is multiplied by the supplier's minimum water-wet bubble point: PBPmin = WBPmin × (PBPavg/WBPavg). The difference between product and water comes from differing properties such as surface tension, so a ratio is used for conversion, not subtraction; the inverted-ratio formulas are also wrong.

questions.question: What steam sterilization temperature are most sterilizing filters confirmed by the manufacturer to withstand?

options.A: At least 121°C, with some up to 130-134°C
options.B: Only up to 105°C, above which they deform
options.C: At least 140°C, to ensure a 10^-6 SAL
options.D: They cannot be steam sterilized, only treated with 80°C hot water

questions.explanation: Section 8.1.1 states that most sterilizing filters are confirmed by the manufacturer to withstand steam sterilization at least at 121°C, with some up to 130-134°C; higher temperatures may destabilize the filter plastics, affect integrity, or increase extractables. Sterilization validation demonstrates a 10^-6 SAL with BIs and a post-sterilization integrity test, not by raising the temperature to 140°C.

questions.question: What does TR26 recommend for the cool-down phase of SIP?

options.A: Quickly flush the filter housing with cold water to shorten the overall cycle time
options.B: Maintain positive pressure with a gas such as air; gas cooling is preferable to liquid
options.C: Open all valves and let the system naturally draw in room air to equalize pressure
options.D: Feed steam in from the downstream side in reverse to offset the pressure differential caused by upstream cooling

questions.explanation: Section 8.1.2 states that during cooling, air or another suitable gas should be used to maintain positive pressure across the filter; if the upstream cools faster than the cartridge, an excessive reverse pressure differential can result. Gas cooling is preferable to liquid cooling because the latter can cause thermal shock that damages the filter. TR26 does not recommend letting the system draw in air naturally; feeding steam in reverse at high differential pressure is exactly the cause of damage mentioned in section 5.8.2.

questions.question: Which statement about the scope of application of SIP (sterilize-in-place) is correct?

options.A: Any disposable capsule with a polypropylene or polyester housing can be directly pressurized-steam sterilized in line
options.B: As long as the temperature is sufficient, SIP does not need pressure gauges upstream and downstream to monitor differential pressure
options.C: It is limited to housings that can withstand steam pressure of 15-30 psig (1-2 bar); capsules with polypropylene housings are generally not suitable
options.D: SIP can be used only for filter assemblies that have first been gamma irradiation sterilized

questions.explanation: Section 8.1.2 states that SIP is limited to filters in housings that can withstand 15-30 psig (1-2 bar) steam pressure; disposable capsules with polypropylene or polyester housings should not be subjected to in-line pressurized steam (with exceptions for high-temperature polymers such as polyetherimide). During SIP, pressure gauges should be fitted upstream and downstream of the filter and the differential pressure limit observed; steam sterilizing a filter that has already been irradiated is in fact a risk.

questions.question: If a filter that has already been gamma irradiation sterilized is sterilized again by steam, what risk does TR26 point out?

options.A: There is no risk; a second sterilization further raises sterility assurance
options.B: It only makes the membrane easier to wet, which benefits the integrity test
options.C: Reaction products such as ethylene chlorohydrin remain in the filter material
options.D: It may increase extractables/leachables and compromise integrity

questions.explanation: Section 8.2 states that most irradiation-sterilized filters have not been validated to withstand a second irradiation or steam sterilization; steam sterilizing a previously irradiated filter may increase extractables/leachables and cause loss of integrity (which can be confirmed with an integrity test). Section 8.4 also explains that autoclaving after irradiation may not be feasible and should be confirmed with the manufacturer. Ethylene chlorohydrin is an issue of ethylene oxide sterilization.

questions.question: Which statement about sterilizing filters with ethylene oxide is consistent with TR26?

options.A: It is very suitable for large pleated cartridges, because the gas can easily penetrate the membrane
options.B: The filter should be kept moist during sterilization to help the gas and water vapor interact
options.C: Spores of Geobacillus stearothermophilus are the preferred BI
options.D: Because gas has difficulty getting in and out of the membrane, it is generally used only for very small encapsulated disc filters

questions.explanation: Section 8.3 states that because it is difficult to ensure gas gets in and out of the membrane, EtO is generally not used for pleated filters, only for very small encapsulated disc filters; during sterilization the filter should be kept dry, and the packaging must allow water vapor and gas in and allow residues to be removed. The EtO biological indicator preferred by TR26 is Bacillus atrophaeus spores, not Geobacillus stearothermophilus.

questions.question: According to Appendix I, what is the relationship between diffusive flow and membrane pore size below the bubble point?

options.A: The larger the pore size, the larger the diffusive flow, in linear proportion
options.B: When the pores are filled with liquid, it is independent of pore size
options.C: The smaller the pore size, the larger the diffusive flow, in inverse proportion
options.D: Diffusive flow is proportional to the fourth power of pore size

questions.explanation: Equation 4 shows that diffusive flux depends on the diffusion coefficient and solubility of the gas in the wetting liquid, pressure differential, porosity, and wet layer thickness; as long as the pores are filled with wetting liquid, diffusive flux is independent of the actual pore size. What is proportional to the fourth power of pore size is viscous flow above the bubble point, following Hagen-Poiseuille (Equation 6).

questions.question: Under what circumstances does the linear relationship described by Equation 5 (F = K1·P) no longer hold?

options.A: When the test gas is changed from air to nitrogen
options.B: When the test temperature is below 20°C
options.C: In large systems where the total membrane area exceeds 1 m²
options.D: When the pressure exceeds the bubble point

questions.explanation: Equation 5 predicts that diffusive flow is linear with test pressure; once the test pressure exceeds the pressure needed to push the wetting liquid out of the pores (the bubble point of the largest pore), bulk/viscous flow appears in addition to diffusive flow and the linear relationship no longer holds. Changing the gas changes the size of K1 but does not break linearity; temperature and area likewise affect only the values.

questions.question: According to Laplace's bubble point equation (Equation 7: P = 4kγcosθ/d), which statement is correct?

options.A: The larger the pore size, the lower the pressure required to push out the wetting liquid
options.B: The greater the surface tension of the wetting liquid, the lower the bubble point
options.C: Bubble point pressure is proportional to the maximum pore size
options.D: Bubble point is proportional to the solubility of the test gas

questions.explanation: Equation 7 shows that the pressure to open a pore is inversely proportional to pore diameter d and proportional to surface tension γ, the cosine of the contact angle cosθ, and the shape factor k, so larger pores are pushed open earlier. Greater surface tension raises rather than lowers the bubble point; gas solubility affects diffusive flow and is not in this equation (Appendix II also points out that bubble point is unaffected by gas type).

questions.question: Beyond the bubble point of the largest pore, which equation is commonly used to model viscous flow of gas through the emptied pores?

options.A: Fick's law of diffusion
options.B: Henry's law of solubility
options.C: The Hagen-Poiseuille equation
options.D: The Arrhenius rate equation

questions.explanation: Appendix I states that after the liquid is expelled, viscous flow of gas through these pores follows the laws of viscous transport and is commonly modeled with the Hagen-Poiseuille equation for flow in cylindrical tubes (Equation 6). Fick's law and Henry's law describe the process below the bubble point in which gas dissolves and diffuses through the wetted membrane; Arrhenius is unrelated.

questions.question: How are the constant K2 in Equation 8 (d = K2/P) and the relationship between bubble point and retention capability established?

options.A: Empirically, because K2 covers pore shape and the wetting characteristics of a specific membrane/liquid combination
options.B: They can be calculated directly from pore sizes measured by SEM, with no experiments or challenge tests needed at all
options.C: All membrane materials and wetting liquid combinations share the same universal K2 value
options.D: They are determined by the diffusion coefficient and solubility of the test gas in the wetting liquid

questions.explanation: K2 is a correction factor that covers both the shape of the largest pore and the wetting characteristics of the specific membrane/wetting liquid combination, so both the constant and the relationship between bubble point and retention of specific contaminants must be established empirically. K2 differs for different membrane and liquid combinations; diffusion coefficient and solubility are parameters of diffusive flow.

questions.question: What is the most common error in reading a manual bubble point test?

options.A: Raising the pressure too slowly, so that the measured bubble point is systematically too high
options.B: Downstream tubing that is too short, so bubbles do not have time to appear at the liquid surface
options.C: Mistaking stray bubbles caused by diffusion for bulk flow and calling it too early
options.D: Using nitrogen instead of air, which distorts the bubble point

questions.explanation: Appendix II states that the most common error is misjudging bubbles that are not caused by bulk flow as the bubble point; some bubbles result from gas diffusing through the wetted membrane, and the determination should be based on free flowing gas, not the first bubble. Overshoot is caused by raising pressure too quickly; downstream tubing should be as little and unkinked as possible; and bubble point is not affected by the type of gas.

questions.question: Which statement about the influence of test gas type on integrity test limits is correct?

options.A: Limits for diffusive flow/pressure hold depend on the gas type; bubble point is not affected by gas type
options.B: None of the three tests is affected by gas type, so limits for air and nitrogen can be used interchangeably, with no need to establish or convert them separately
options.C: Only bubble point is affected by gas type, while the diffusive flow test is unaffected
options.D: Simply switching to nitrogen allows the diffusive flow limit for air to be used directly and relaxed by 10%

questions.explanation: Section 11.2 explains that for a correct determination the right limit must be used for the gas type, which applies only to diffusion/pressure hold tests; bubble point is unaffected by gas type. The reason is that diffusive flow depends on the solubility and diffusion coefficient of the gas in the wetting liquid, while bubble point depends on surface tension, contact angle, and pore size. Section 7.4.2 also notes that diffusive flow acceptance criteria are specific to a particular test gas.

questions.question: Why do filter manufacturers generally not publish the allowable pressure drop for a pressure hold/decay test?

options.A: Because pressure hold cannot be correlated with bacterial retention in any way
options.B: Because the pressure drop depends only on the pore size rating, so the user can simply look it up
options.C: Because this test is used only in development and not for production filters
options.D: Because the pressure drop depends on the upstream volume and test time of the specific assembly and must be calculated separately

questions.explanation: Section 11.3 states that the allowable pressure drop is unique to a specific filter assembly and piping system, and must be calculated from the diffusive flow specification at a given pressure and constant temperature, the upstream system volume, and the test time, so the upstream volume must be determined first. Pressure hold is correlated with bacterial retention indirectly through its relationship to the diffusive flow test, and is often used before use (after sterilization) and after filtration.

questions.question: What effect does the upstream volume have on a pressure hold/decay test?

options.A: The larger the upstream volume, the higher the test sensitivity, so making it as large as possible is recommended
options.B: The larger the volume, the lower the sensitivity, but the smaller it is, the more susceptible to temperature change
options.C: Upstream volume does not affect results, only the stabilization time needed before the test
options.D: The smaller the upstream volume, the less the test is affected by temperature fluctuation

questions.explanation: Section 11.3 states that the sensitivity of pressure hold falls as the upstream system volume increases, so keeping the upstream volume as small as possible is recommended; TR26 also cautions that the smaller the upstream volume, the more sensitive it is to temperature change, so temperature must be kept stable during the test. Upstream volume also lengthens the stabilization time needed, but that is not its only effect.

questions.question: How does an automated integrity tester determine the bubble point, and what are the requirements for its qualification?

options.A: By the first bubble to appear; after factory calibration by the supplier no separate qualification is needed
options.B: By the point where pressure decay under stepwise pressure increases becomes nonlinear; it must be qualified against an independent reference method
options.C: By the volume of gas collected in a downstream graduated cylinder; only an external calibration once a year is needed, with no other qualification
options.D: By a sudden rise in filtrate turbidity; the filter supplier is responsible for confirming instrument performance

questions.explanation: Section 11.4 explains that automated instruments determine the bubble point with a pressure hold/decay test under stepwise pressure increases, and the point at which the pressure drop becomes nonlinear (according to each instrument maker's algorithm) is the bubble point; diffusive flow is converted from pressure drop or measured directly with an upstream mass flow meter. Whatever technology is used, the instrument must be qualified against an independent reference method. The "first bubble" is exactly the common error of manual reading.

questions.question: When investigating a failure of a manual integrity test, what three items does Appendix III list for consideration?

options.A: Insufficient wetting, inappropriate wetting medium (for example solvent instead of water), and incorrect filter pore size rating
options.B: Excessive bioburden, abnormal product pH, and batch size exceeding the validated maximum volume
options.C: Excessive sterilization temperature, biological indicator failure, and outer packaging damaged in transport
options.D: Operators not gowned, abnormal cleanroom pressure differential, and temperature and humidity outside specification

questions.explanation: For manual test failures, Appendix III lists three items: insufficiently wetted filter, inappropriate wetting medium (such as solvent instead of water), and incorrect filter pore size rating. These are all causes in the test itself, not real damage to the membrane; the other options are process or environmental deviations and are not integrity test troubleshooting items listed in Appendix III.

questions.topic: Why automated testing is more reproducible
questions.question: Why does Appendix III consider that automated test instruments may be more reproducible than manual testing?

options.A: Automated instruments use a much lower test pressure than manual testing
options.B: Automated instruments avoid human subjective judgment
options.C: Automated instruments do not need to wet the filter before testing
options.D: Automated instruments are completely unaffected by changes in ambient temperature

questions.explanation: Section 12.0 states that automated test devices avoid human subjectivity and may therefore be more reproducible (Appendix II also mentions that manual bubble point reading varies with the operator). Automated instruments still require the filter to be fully wetted, and Table 12.0-1 lists temperature drift in several places as a cause of faults, so they are not unaffected by temperature; test pressure is determined by the method and the filter.

questions.question: When an automated test shows "No Pressure Decay" (no pressure drop at all), what possible cause does Table 12.0-1 list?

options.A: Damaged filter membrane
options.B: Inappropriate wetting liquid (solvent instead of water)
options.C: Incorrect filter pore size rating
options.D: Downstream valve closed or temperature rising during the test

questions.explanation: For No Pressure Decay, Table 12.0-1 lists: improperly installed inlet tubing, downstream valve closed, blocked connections, blocked internal gas path, and temperature rising during the test. A damaged membrane, inappropriate wetting liquid, or wrong pore size would cause an excessive pressure drop or diffusive flow failure, not a complete absence of pressure drop. These causes all relate to piping, valves, gas path, or temperature rather than the membrane itself.

questions.question: In Table 12.0-1, for which fault is "Large multiple-cartridge assembly" listed as a possible cause?

options.A: No Test Pressure Build-Up
options.B: Continuous Venting of the Unit
options.C: Failure of Bubble Point
options.D: Measured Volume is Wrong

questions.explanation: Large multiple-cartridge assembly appears only under Failure of Bubble Point. The reason is consistent with section 7.1.1: at very large areas, the large background diffusive flow below the bubble point masks the transition to bulk flow, making bubble point reading inaccurate, so large systems generally switch to diffusive flow. The causes of the other three are leaks, valve contamination, wrongly set reference volume, and so on.

questions.question: When an automated test aborts during the "upstream volume test" phase, which is one possible cause listed in Table 12.0-1?

options.A: The filter pore size is too small, so gas cannot pass at all
options.B: The test gas purity is too high, making the pressure reading unstable
options.C: The upstream volume of the filter system is too large, or the external reference volume is improperly connected
options.D: The product concentration is too high, raising the filtrate viscosity

questions.explanation: For Abortion During Upstream Volume Test, Table 12.0-1 lists: upstream volume too large, external reference volume improperly connected, internal gas path leaks, filter failure, insufficient stabilization time, and insufficient wetting. The other options are not in the table. This also echoes the reminder in Appendix II on pressure hold: the upstream volume must be correctly determined and kept as small as possible, and large volumes need longer stabilization time.
